newsitem.title: PANAMA: Tiomin says Panama mining project not threatened.
newsitem.headline: Tiomin says Panama mining project not threatened.

text.p: Canadian mining company Tiomin Resources Inc said the creation of an Indian homeland would not affect its major copper mining project in Panama.
Tiomin plans to mine the world's 12th largest copper deposit in Cerro Colorado, 220 miles (350 km) from Panama City.
It is now located inside an Indian homeland, or comarca, after the unanimous approval by Panama's Congress on Tuesday of the creation of a sovereign homeland for Ngobe-Bugle indians.
The comarca will be signed into law by President Ernesto Perez Balladares next month.

"We will go ahead," Michael Shaw, Tiomin's vice president for Panama, said. "We have a concession to exploit a mine. The mineral below the surface doesn't belong to the comarca, but to the Panamanian people."
Shaw said Tiomin saw the comarca "as an opportunity to work with one governing body. In the past, there were scattered groups all claiming to speak for the Ngobe-Bugle Indians."
After a 25-year battle, Panamanian lawmakers approved the sovereign homeland for the nation's largest Indian group of nearly 1.72 million acres (700,000 hectares).
Hector Huertas, an attorney representating the group, said that once signed into law, Panama will recognize the traditional government of the Ngobe-Bugle which numbers some 125,000.
But the Ngobe-Bugle will continue to fight the mining project, he said.
"While the Indians see the comarca as an achievement, they see the mine as a threat to their environment, society, culture and economic livelihood," he said.
On March 15, Tiomin is expected to present to the Panamanian government the results of a pre-feasability study on whether they will continue the project, Shaw said.
